intro:
This track is about what goes wrong once a system runs on more than one machine, and how to reason about it anyway. By the end you can say what a timeout does and doesn't tell you, pick the right clock for a timestamp and for a duration, make a paused process harmless with fencing tokens, order events that share no clock, name the system model an algorithm is proved against, and test a distributed design in layers, from a model checker to a seeded simulator that replays any failure exactly.

You need the Replication track (leaders, followers and failover) and the Transactions track (atomicity, lost updates) first. The Consistency and consensus track comes next and builds directly on lessons 5 to 8 here: linearizability, consensus and Raft all assume the fault model this track sets up.

Seven of the eight labs are plain Kotlin simulations in the `sim` module: a seeded scheduler on a virtual clock, with no Docker, so a run with crashes, pauses and partitions takes milliseconds and comes out the same every time. The tests use JUnit and jqwik property tests. Lesson 5's lab takes a real Redis lock in the `redis` module and needs Docker. Run a lab from the `labs` folder with `./gradlew :sim:test --tests 'sfz.dist.lNN.*'` (lesson 5: `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.dist.l05.*'`).
cheatsheet:
## Partial failure (lesson 1)

Silence after a request has six causes that look the same from the caller: request lost, request queued, remote crashed, remote paused, reply lost, reply slow. Every remote call has three outcomes: yes, no and unknown.

| Fact | Consequence |
|---|---|
| TCP's ACK means the remote kernel got the bytes | It is not an application answer |
| TCP removes duplicates within one connection | A retry on a new connection is a new request |
| Packet networks queue in switches, kernels, hypervisors and TCP | Delay has no upper bound; no timeout separates slow from dead |
| A retry repeats the side effect | Send an idempotency key made once per operation; store it in the same transaction as the effect |

## Detecting failure (lesson 2)

- A timeout trades detection time against false alarms. Pick it from measured delays, or adapt: TCP's RTO is the smoothed RTT plus 4 times its variation; phi accrual turns recent heartbeat gaps into a suspicion level.
- SWIM asks k other members to probe before it accuses, marks a node suspect before dead, and lets it refute with a higher incarnation number. Lifeguard makes a struggling accuser slow down.
- Gray failure: users see errors, the detector sees a healthy node. Judge health on the request path.
- A paused node looks exactly like a dead one. Detectors only suspect; correctness comes from majorities and fencing.

## Clocks (lesson 3)

| Clock | JVM | Use for | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wall clock | `System.currentTimeMillis()`, `Instant.now()` | points in time, timestamps for people | jumps back and forward (NTP steps, VM migration) |
| Monotonic | `System.nanoTime()` | durations, timeouts | meaningless across machines and reboots |

Quartz drifts up to about 200 ppm (about 17 s a day). NTP over the internet: tens of ms. On AWS, under 100 µs over NTP and under 40 µs with the PTP hardware clock. Last write wins with client timestamps drops a causally later write whenever the writer's clock lags by more than the gap between the writes. Spanner commits only after waiting out the clock's error bound; CockroachDB assumes a maximum offset (500 ms by default) and shuts down nodes that exceed it. Inject skew in tests through `java.time.Clock`.

## Pauses, leases and fencing (lessons 4 and 5)

- A process can stop between any two instructions, for seconds, and can't tell: GC, hypervisor steal or live migration, CPU-quota throttling, swapping, `SIGSTOP`, synchronous I/O. ZGC pauses are under a millisecond on JDK 25; the other causes don't care which collector you run.
- A lease is a lock that runs out: `SET key token NX PX ttl` in Redis, a TTL lease in etcd, a session in ZooKeeper. Release with compare-and-delete, never plain `DEL`.
- Check, then act, always has a gap. Renewal and re-checking shrink it; nothing inside the holder closes it.
- **Fencing token**: a number that grows with every grant (Redis `INCR`, etcd revision, ZooKeeper zxid, an epoch) and travels with every write. The resource refuses any token lower than the highest it has seen. Only the resource can stop a stale holder.

## Ordering without a shared clock (lesson 6)

| Stamp or id | Order it promises | It can't tell you |
|---|---|---|
| Wall-clock timestamp | none across machines | cause before effect, once skew exceeds the message delay |
| Lamport (counter, node) | causes before effects; a total order | real time; whether two events were concurrent |
| Vector clock | causes before effects, and which events are concurrent | it costs one counter per node |
| Hybrid logical clock | Lamport's guarantee in 64 bits, close to wall time | real-time order of events no message connects |
| UUIDv7, Snowflake, ULID | time order within one generator at most | order across generators |
| One counter (sequence, TiDB's oracle) or bounded clocks with commit wait | real-time order | it costs a round trip to the counter, or the wait |

## System models (lesson 7)

| Timing model | What you may assume |
|---|---|
| Synchronous | known bounds on delay, pauses and clock error (no real system has them) |
| Partially synchronous | bounds usually hold but can be broken for a while (the realistic one) |
| Asynchronous | no bounds, no clocks, no timeouts |

| Node model | A faulty node |
|---|---|
| Crash-stop | stops and never comes back |
| Crash-recovery | restarts; keeps what it fsynced, loses memory (the realistic one) |
| Byzantine | does anything, including lie |

- Safety: nothing bad ever happens; must hold in every execution. Liveness: something good eventually happens; may wait for timing to behave. "Eventually" means liveness.
- FLP: with no timing assumptions and one possible crash, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee that it finishes. Raft and Paxos stay safe always and use timeouts for progress.
- Write anything another node may count (a vote, an acknowledgement) to disk before you send it.
- Crash faults: 2f + 1 nodes. Byzantine faults: 3f + 1 (PBFT, quorums of 2f + 1). Most databases skip BFT; they use checksums (CRC-32C, end to end), validation and access control against small lies.

## Testing (lesson 8)

| Method | Checks | Misses |
|---|---|---|
| TLA+, P (model checking) | the design, every schedule of a small model | bugs in the code; bugs that need a bigger model |
| Deterministic simulation (FoundationDB, TigerBeetle's VOPR, Antithesis) | the real code, millions of seeded runs that replay exactly | faults and workloads nobody put in the simulator |
| Jepsen and Elle | the deployed system under real faults, from the client history | what no client observes; it can't prove absence |
| Property tests (jqwik, Kotest) | one component on generated inputs, shrunk to a minimal failure | interactions between components |
| Fault injection (Toxiproxy), chaos experiments | your service and your operations under one real fault | rare combinations of faults |

A simulator is only deterministic if every random choice and every clock read goes through the seed: run one seed twice and compare the whole trace.
recap: A distributed system fails in part, and a node knows only the messages it has received: silence has six causes, and every remote call can end in unknown. Idempotency keys make retries safe.

Failure detectors turn silence into suspicion. Pick timeouts from measured delays or let them adapt (phi accrual, SWIM with Lifeguard), and expect them to be wrong: correctness must come from majorities and fencing.

Wall clocks give points in time and jump; monotonic clocks give durations. Anything that orders writes by timestamp is only as good as its clock bound: last write wins loses writes, Spanner waits out the bound.
A process can stop for seconds at any instruction (GC, VM stalls, throttling, I/O) without knowing, so a lease holder can act after its lease ran out.
Leases need fencing tokens: the resource refuses any token lower than the highest it has seen. Only the resource can stop a stale holder.

Lamport and hybrid logical clocks put causes before effects, vector clocks detect concurrency, and only one counter or a bounded clock with a wait gives real-time order. Time-ordered ids order one generator at most.
Algorithms are proved against a system model; the realistic one is partial synchrony with crash-recovery. Safety must always hold, liveness may wait for timing (FLP), and lying nodes need 3f + 1.
Test in layers: model checking for the design, deterministic simulation for the code, Jepsen-style testing for the deployed system, plus property tests, fault injection and chaos experiments.

quiz.q: A payment request to the card issuer times out after 2 seconds. What do you know about the payment?
options: The issuer is down, so the payment failed
The card was not charged, so a plain retry is safe
Nothing for certain: the request or the reply may be lost or late, or the issuer may be paused or crashed, so the charge may or may not have happened
The network dropped the request
quiz.why: Silence fits six situations, and in two of them (reply lost, reply slow) the issuer charged the card. The caller can't tell which from its side, so the outcome is unknown. That's why a retry must carry the same idempotency key, so the issuer can recognise it. Concluding the payment failed, the most tempting option, is how cards get charged twice.

quiz.q: Your service retries a timed-out payment over a fresh TCP connection. Why doesn't TCP stop the issuer from charging twice?
options: TCP removes duplicates only within one connection; the retry is a new request on a new connection
TCP never removes duplicate segments
TCP would stop it, but only if Nagle's algorithm is off
TLS turns off TCP's duplicate detection
quiz.why: TCP's sequence numbers remove duplicate segments inside one connection, and its ACK means only that the remote kernel received the bytes. A retry after a timeout usually opens a new connection, and to the issuer's application it is a brand-new request. Only an application-level idempotency key, stored with the effect, makes the retry safe.

quiz.q: Your cluster declares a node dead after 3 seconds without a heartbeat, and the JVMs occasionally pause for 5 seconds. What follows?
options: Nothing, because heartbeats are sent from a separate thread
The detector will sometimes declare a live, paused node dead, so correctness can't depend on the detector being right
The paused node will notice the pause and stop itself in time
Phi accrual would never make this mistake
quiz.why: A paused process sends nothing, so from outside it looks exactly like a crashed one. Any detector faster than the longest pause will sometimes suspect a node that is alive, and an adaptive detector such as phi accrual only makes the trade smarter, not free. The heartbeat thread stops with the rest of the JVM, and a process learns of its pause only after it resumes. So the system must stay correct when the detector is wrong: majorities and fencing.

quiz.q: Health checks for an authorization service are all green, yet about 5% of requests fail, all through one faulty network path. What should change?
options: Lower the health-check timeout
Add more replicas of the service
Send health checks more often
Judge health from the real request path, with real or synthetic requests, instead of a separate check
quiz.why: This is gray failure: the detector and the users see different things, because the health check doesn't travel the path that is broken. Checking faster or with a shorter timeout repeats the same blind check, and more replicas behind the same path don't help. Health measured on the request path, as users experience it, sees the failure.

quiz.q: Which JVM call should measure how long the call to the issuer took?
options: `System.nanoTime()`
`System.currentTimeMillis()`
`Instant.now()`
`LocalDateTime.now()`
quiz.why: `nanoTime` reads a monotonic clock, which never jumps, so the difference of two readings is a true duration. The other three read the wall clock, which NTP or a VM migration can step forward or back in the middle of the call, giving a duration that is too long, too short or negative. The wall clock is for points in time, not intervals.

quiz.q: Two services update one row in a store that keeps the write with the highest client timestamp (last write wins). Service B's clock runs 5 s behind. B reads A's value and writes a new one 1 s later. What happens?
options: B's write wins, because it happened later
Both writes are kept as siblings for the application to merge
B's write carries the older timestamp and is silently dropped, although B was told it succeeded
The store rejects B's write with a clock-skew error
quiz.why: Last write wins compares timestamps, not causality. B's clock says its write happened about 4 seconds before A's, so the store keeps A's value and throws B's away after acknowledging it. Siblings need version vectors, and few stores check skew on writes. Jepsen's 2013 Cassandra test lost about 28% of acknowledged writes to last write wins.

quiz.q: A worker checks that its lease is valid, then a 15-second VM stall hits before it writes, and meanwhile another worker takes the lease and writes. What stops the first worker's late write?
options: A lease of 60 seconds instead of 10
The storage refusing the write because its fencing token is lower than one it has already seen
Checking the lease once more right before the write
Running the JVM with ZGC
quiz.why: The pause landed after the last check, so nothing inside the worker can catch it, and no lease length is safe against an unbounded pause. A second check narrows the gap but a pause can still fall after it, and ZGC doesn't help with a VM stall. The resource is the only party that sees both writes, so it must compare tokens: the new holder's token is higher, and the stale one is refused.

quiz.q: Events a and b happened on different nodes, and no chain of messages connects them. What do their Lamport timestamps tell you?
options: Which of them happened first in real time
That they were concurrent
That a happened first, if L(a) < L(b)
Nothing about their real order: either can have the smaller stamp, and only vector clocks show they were concurrent
quiz.why: Lamport stamps promise one direction only: if a happened before b, then L(a) < L(b). For unrelated events the order of the stamps is an accident of counting, so L(a) < L(b) doesn't mean a came first, and the stamps can't reveal concurrency at all. Vector clocks can, at the cost of one counter per node. Real-time order across unconnected events needs one counter or a bounded clock with a wait.

quiz.q: A consensus node records its vote in memory, replies, and writes the vote to disk a few milliseconds later. In which node model is that safe?
options: Crash-stop only
Crash-recovery
Every model, because the gap is only milliseconds
Byzantine, since votes are signed
quiz.why: Under crash-stop a node that crashes in the gap never comes back, so its vote can't be cast twice. Under crash-recovery, a crash between the reply and the write makes the node restart without the vote and vote again, which can elect two leaders in one term. A short gap only makes the bug rare, not impossible. Raft requires the vote on stable storage before the reply.

quiz.q: A replicated message broker acknowledges messages at once but fsyncs only every two minutes by default. Which testing method is most likely to reveal that it loses acknowledged messages?
options: A property-based test of its message encoder
Jepsen-style testing with a nemesis that simulates power loss by dropping unsynced writes
A TLA+ model of its replication protocol
Unit tests of each node's request handler
quiz.why: The bug lives in the deployed configuration, not in the design or one component: the protocol may be correct, but the default fsync interval breaks its assumption that acknowledged data is on disk. A black-box test that kills nodes and drops unsynced writes, as Jepsen did to NATS with LazyFS, exposes it. A TLA+ model would assume durable writes, and the encoder and handlers are fine on their own.
